the workload of lung cancer specialist nurses is not associated with the number of patients they care for, but with the number of other nurses they work with and the facilities they have to treat patients.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the lung cancer specialist nurse (LCSN) in cancer care.
the role of specialist cancer nurses in the UK, and the barriers to them being able to deliver the best quality of care.
the role and impact of lung cancer nurses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
LCNS are an important part of the lung cancer care pathway and that the workload of the LCNS is a major factor in the delivery of care.
the findings of this study suggest that there is a lack of consistency in the provision of lung cancer nursing services across England.

the working practices of lung cancer nurse specialists vary according to service characteristics, most frequently associated to anti-cancer treatment facilities, but also to the size of the lung cancer services and to the presence of other specialist nurses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are barriers to delivering advanced cancer nurse practice in the English lung cancer service.
LCNS working practices vary across England, and that the most common intervention not being routinely offered by LCNS is proactive case management.
LCNS working practices are associated with service factors, most often with anti cancer treatment facilities, and are not associated with caseload, service size, or patient survival.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no one size fits all solution.
LCNS workload is not associated with service factors such as trust size or patient survival, but is associated with chemotherapy facilities and lack of administrative support.
there are many barriers to advanced cancer nursing practice.
